newsitem.title: CHINA: China says no one poisoned in cyanide spill.
newsitem.headline: China says no one poisoned in cyanide spill.

text.p: No deaths or illnesses have been reported following a cyanide spill in a south China river, but fish are dying and some local water companies have suspended supplies, official Chinese media said on Friday.

The Liberation Daily said 19 barrels had ruptured when a truck carrying 10 tonnes of cyanide in 200 barrels fell into the Guijiang River near Wuzhou city in southwestern Guangxi province late Monday night.
Quoting the Guangxi Daily, the newspaper said fish in the river had begun dying but no people had been poisoned.
One barrel of the poison was still missing, it said.
Three people in the truck, including the driver and the owner of the cyanide, suffered minor injuries when the vehicle plunged into the river and had been detained, it said.
Two water works in Wuzhou had stopped taking water from the Guijiang, and city authorities were checking fish and vegetables for traces of the poison, it said, adding that local citizens were calm.
The Guijiang is a tributary of the Pearl River, which flows through heavily-populated Guangdong province and into the South China Sea near Hong Kong and Macau.
The water company in the Portuguese-administered territory of Macau said on Thursday it had suspended water imports from China, and that local water reserves were safe.
A spokeswoman from Hong Kong's water department said the water supply there was not in danger as the water imported from China was from another tributary of the Pearl River system.
Macau banned people from bringing food in from China while Hong Kong launched cyanide checks.
With scarce land resources, both Hong Kong and Macau rely on imported food, mostly from China.
Health checks on food imports are routinely carried out to guard against such things as pesticide poisoning, but the cyanide checks are new to Hong Kong.
A Wuzhou official told Hong Kong radio on Thursday that the chemical was intended for electroplating.
